commentary.seminaVerbi:
David’s lion-play and songcraft sit near the Hindu kshatriya ideal where ferocity is disciplined into dharma, and near the Bhagavad Gita’s pivot from violence to consecration: the hand that strikes is trained to offer. The singers before the altar resemble the Sufi use of sama and qawwali, where melody is not ornament but a technology of attention that tames the self into gratitude.

Herod’s birthday feast is a courtroom of mirrors: desire, pride, and audience fuse into a single compulsion. That psychology matches the Greek tragic engine—Agamemnon bound by honor, Creon by public face—where a vow becomes a trapdoor and the crowd is the hidden god. Speculation: John’s severed head on a platter echoes the Buddhist warning about courtly intoxication, the “honey on the razor’s edge,” pleasure that demands blood to keep its spell.
commentary.excursus:
Sirach sells David as purified fat, a choice cut trimmed for sacred use: violence rendered hygienic by music. The text wants you to believe that killing can be transmuted into sweetness, that a sling-stone can become a hymn. Desire is recruited as liturgy; the warrior’s appetite is baptized into “thanks.” The dread is what’s omitted: the same hand that breaks horns can also take what it wants, and the singers are set before the altar like a curtain to soften the sound of conquest.

Mark shows the cost when violence can’t be aestheticized. Herod isn’t a monster; he’s a man split in two, aroused by a girl’s dance and haunted by a prophet’s voice. John functions as Herod’s conscience and as his fetish: he “hears him willingly,” keeps him close, like a dangerous purity he can’t stop touching. Herodias understands the psychology perfectly: you don’t defeat a ruler with argument, you corner him inside his own performance.

The banquet is the anti-psalm. An oath replaces prayer, applause replaces blessing, and the head arrives as the true centerpiece, served up to stabilize male status in front of male peers. The girl is the instrument, but the desire is Herod’s: he turns lust into law, then calls himself bound. John dies not for truth but for a room’s hunger for a clean ending. And the final dread is that everyone gets what they want: the prophet’s purity becomes an object, the king keeps his face, the mother gets her trophy, and the disciples are left with only a body—no music, no metaphor, just weight.
commentary.synthesis: God grants rule and strength only as delegated instrumentality, and he judges rulers who convert conscience into theater. The just man’s word stands; the court’s oaths and feasts rot into murder.

gospel.text: The court’s competing identifications of Jesus function as a diagnostic: when authority lacks truth, it compensates with classifications—names standing in for repentance.
The imprisonment is explicitly tethered to an illicit union; the narrative locates the state’s violence in private disorder that has been enthroned.

A chain of mediated wills replaces judgment: pleasure prompts an oath, an oath yields to an audience, and the audience becomes the real sovereign; the prophet is killed so the ruler can remain unembarrassed.
The disciples’ burial is the sole act of sanity in the episode: a quiet refusal to let the regime’s spectacle be the last word.

reading.text: David’s public glory is depicted as doxological capital: victory is immediately converted into praise, so the king’s legitimacy is framed as derivative—his renown is permitted only as it returns to the Lord.
The text treats political security (“enemies on every side”) as an achieved condition, yet it refuses to let that condition be self-grounding; it is narrated as a consequence, not a foundation.
Inner disposition is made the hinge of outward power: thanksgiving and whole-hearted love are presented as the grammar in which kingship can be spoken without becoming idolatry.

marginalia.text: Election rendered as butchery: fat trimmed, choice revealed.
Predation domesticated; the shepherd toys with teeth.
A hand lifts; a pebble legislates against boasting.
Prayer transfers agency; the right hand becomes an instrument, not a cause.
From slaughter to liturgy: the altar gets musicians as policy.
A guilty court invents resurrection to explain rumor.
The verb remembers: “I beheaded” outlives the head.
Law spoken plainly; illegality needs no ornament.
“Convenient day”: the calendar conspires with appetite.
A kingdom wagered in a room; sovereignty traded for applause.
Speed as complicity: haste makes murder administrative.
The platter circulates; death becomes a gift economy.

lines: And as the fat taken away from the flesh, so was David chosen from among the children of Israel.
He played with lions as with lambs: and with bears he did in like manner as with the lambs of the flock, in his youth.
Did not he kill the giant, and take away reproach from his people?
In lifting up his hand, with the stone in the sling he beat down the boasting of Goliath:
For he called upon the Lord the Almighty, and he gave strength in his right hand, to take away the mighty warrior, and to set up the horn of his nation.
So in ten thousand did he glorify him, and praised him in the blessings of the Lord, in offering to him a crown of glory:
For he destroyed the enemies on every side, and extirpated the Philistines the adversaries unto this day: he broke their horn for ever.
In all his works he gave thanks to the holy one, and to the most High, with words of glory.
With his whole heart he praised the Lord, and loved God that made him: and he gave him power against his enemies:
And he set singers before the altar, and by their voices he made sweet melody.

lines: And king Herod heard, (for his name was made manifest,) and he said: John the Baptist is risen again from dead, and therefore mighty works shew forth themselves in him.
And others said: It is Elias. But others said: It is a prophet, as one of the prophets.
Which Herod hearing, said: John whom I beheaded, he is risen again from the dead.
For Herod himself had sent and apprehended John, and bound him prison for the sake of Herodias the wife of Philip his brother, because he had married her.
For John said to Herod: It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife.
Now Herodias laid snares for him: and was desirous to put him to death and could not.

For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man: and kept him, and when he heard him, did many things: and he heard him willingly. And kept him... That is, from the designs of Herodias; and for fear of the people, would not put him to death, though she sought it; and through her daughter she effected her wish.
And when a convenient day was come, Herod made a supper for his birthday, for the princes, and tribunes, and chief men of Galilee.

And when the daughter of the same Herodias had come in, and had danced, and pleased Herod, and them that were at table with him, the king said to the damsel: Ask of me what thou wilt, and I will give it thee.
And he swore to her: Whatsoever thou shalt ask I will give thee, though it be the half of my kingdom.
Who when she was gone out, said to her mother, What shall I ask? But her mother said: The head of John the Baptist.
And when she was come in immediately with haste to the king, she asked, saying: I will that forthwith thou give me in a dish, the head of John the Baptist.
And the king was struck sad. Yet because of his oath, and because of them that were with him at table, he would not displease her:
But sending an executioner, he commanded that his head should be brought in a dish.
And he beheaded him in the prison, and brought his head in a dish: and gave to the damsel, and the damsel gave it her mother.
Which his disciples hearing came, and took his body, and laid it in a tomb.
